item.title: "Neither cruelty, nor violence, nor torture will make me beg for mercy, because I prefer to die with my head raised high, with unshakeable faith... In my country’s predestination rather than live in submission forsaking my sacred principles."
item.description: Patrice Lumumba became one of the most important voices of African independence at a time when European colonial powers were struggling to maintain control across the continent. Born in 1925 in what was then the Belgian Congo, Lumumba rose from relatively modest beginnings to become a leading figure in the Congolese independence movement. He believed political independence meant little if Congo remained economically dependent on the same foreign interests that had benefited from colonial rule. Belgian rule in Congo had left behind a deeply unequal system. For decades, Congolese people had been denied meaningful political power while the country's enormous mineral wealth benefited Belgium and foreign companies. When Congo finally gained independence on June 30, 1960, Lumumba became its first democratically elected prime minister. At the independence ceremony, he delivered a famous speech describing the humiliation, discrimination and violence Congolese people had experienced under colonialism. His words challenged the more celebratory version of Belgian rule presented at the ceremony and immediately established him as an uncompromising voice for genuine independence. The Cold War made Congo's situation even more dangerous. Lumumba's opponents frequently portrayed him as a communist, while Lumumba insisted that his struggle was fundamentally about Congolese sovereignty and freedom from colonial domination. When the mineral-rich province of Katanga broke away shortly after independence and Western governments refused to provide the assistance he wanted, Lumumba turned to the Soviet Union for help. That decision intensified fears in Washington and Brussels about where Congo might align during the Cold War. Within months, Lumumba was removed from power, arrested and eventually transferred to Katanga. On January 17, 1961, at only 35 years old, he was executed by his Congolese enemies with the involvement of Belgian officials. Belgium formally acknowledged decades later that some of its officials bore "moral responsibility" for the circumstances surrounding his death. - African Archives
